records.decision_reason: The full text is directly relevant to LLM-assisted qualitative coding, human authority, transparency, privacy, and Social Verbatim design, but it is a narrative Debate/review and future-design article. It executes no LLM coding study and explicitly describes LLM integration into Social Verbatim as the next development phase, so it is adjacent rather than core empirical evidence.

Relationship/dependence family.value: Social Verbatim/CS-Transcribe tool-development family; the 15 formative interviews and non-LLM beta are background from the author's prior project, while LLM integration remains proposed future work.
Relationship/dependence family.anchor: Introduction and Social Verbatim section, pp. 196 and 210-212

Research objective.value: Review advances in LLM-assisted qualitative coding, identify methodological, ethical, and epistemological challenges, and derive opportunities and design premises for future LLM integration into Social Verbatim while retaining an active reflexive researcher role.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: theoretical review of LLMs and qualitative coding, with a comparative overview of tools/studies and a design discussion for Social Verbatim
Claimed qualitative methodology.anchor: Abstract, Introduction, comparative Tables 1-2, and Conclusion, pp. 195-213

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Unsystematic narrative review and author-constructed comparison tables. No databases, search strings, date limits, eligibility criteria, screening procedure, included-source count, appraisal method, extraction protocol, or synthesis procedure are reported. The article also summarizes a prior formative Social Verbatim study of 15 potential users, but does not execute or evaluate the proposed LLM coding integration.
Actual operationalized methodology.anchor: whole-paper audit; review discussion pp. 196-210 and Social Verbatim section pp. 210-212

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: not applicable to the narrative review; the reviewed literature includes inductive, deductive, and hybrid coding

Domain.value: qualitative social-science research methods, computer-assisted qualitative coding, and Social Verbatim tool design

Dataset name.value: unspecified literature corpus; background CS-Transcribe/Social Verbatim formative interview study
Dataset name.anchor: whole-paper review audit and Social Verbatim section, p. 210

Public or restricted data.value: source literature is publicly cited; access mix and included corpus are not reported. The 15 background interview transcripts are not released or analyzed as a new dataset in this paper.

Number of documents.value: number of reviewed documents not reported; 15 individual interviews are described as background to the existing Social Verbatim beta

Number of participants.value: No participants in an LLM evaluation; background tool-development study reports 15 interviewees (11 women, 4 men): 7 researchers, 5 researcher-transcribers, and 3 transcribers.

Approximate corpus size.value: not reported for the literature review or background interview corpus

Language.anchor: official PDF pp. 195-196 and journal issue record

Sensitive-data status.value: No primary LLM-processed data in this article. The background user interviews are not characterized for sensitivity; the article treats qualitative-participant privacy, anonymization, and external-model data transfer as central design risks.
Sensitive-data status.anchor: challenges and Social Verbatim sections, pp. 205 and 211-212

Model family.value: No model was executed. The review discusses GPT, Claude, Llama, FLAN, Gemini and other LLM families used in prior studies and tools.

Exact model/version.value: not applicable; no model was run for this article or for the proposed Social Verbatim integration
Exact model/version.anchor: whole-paper audit and future-development statement, pp. 211-212

Prompting strategy.value: No prompt was executed. Prompt engineering and prompt traceability are discussed as prior-work practices and proposed Social Verbatim requirements.
Prompting strategy.anchor: coding review and proposed-design section, pp. 200-212

Fine-tuning or adaptation.value: not applicable; prior-work zero-shot/fine-tuning descriptions are reviewed, but no model is adapted in this article

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: not applicable; Thematic-LM's multi-agent design is reviewed but no agent workflow is executed

Agent roles.value: not applicable; reviewed Thematic-LM roles include coder, aggregator, and reviewer

Human role.value: The author argues that researchers must retain interpretive authority, critically evaluate model suggestions using disciplinary and empirical knowledge, monitor and document processes, revise coding criteria, and actively supervise any future Social Verbatim integration.

Unit of analysis.value: published claims, prior systems/studies, and proposed Social Verbatim design features; no primary LLM-coded unit

Generated outputs.value: Narrative review, comparative tables of LLM coding studies/tools, challenge and human-role synthesis, and a set of future Social Verbatim design premises: open models, prompt traceability, active human supervision, privacy standards, flexibility/interactivity, and data-proximate interfaces.

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Conventional citations and author-constructed tables link summarized claims to named papers. The article reports no reproducible search/extraction trail or source-to-synthesis ledger. Prompt traceability is a proposed future Social Verbatim feature, not an evaluated mechanism.
Evidence/provenance mechanism.anchor: Tables 1-2, whole-paper audit, and proposed-design section pp. 211-212

Automatic metrics.value: none; results from cited studies are summarized but not reanalyzed

Human-evaluation design.value: No evaluation of LLM-assisted coding or of the proposed Social Verbatim integration. Fifteen prior formative interviews informed the existing non-LLM demo/beta features.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: No LLM evaluators; background interviewees comprised 7 researchers, 5 researcher-transcribers, and 3 transcribers

Statistical analysis.value: none reported for the review or proposed LLM integration

Principal results.value: The author concludes that LLMs may increase the efficiency and depth of qualitative coding but cannot replace human interpretation. Reported challenges include black-box opacity, inconsistency and context limits, hallucination, social/cultural bias, privacy and security, and weak replicability. The proposed Social Verbatim direction emphasizes open models, visible prompt traces, active researcher supervision and feedback, privacy protections, flexible task-specific interaction, and interfaces that keep researchers close to data; none of these LLM functions is implemented or empirically evaluated in this paper.
Principal results.anchor: challenges, researcher-role, proposed-design, and Conclusion sections, pp. 204-213

Efficiency or cost results.value: Conceptual claims that LLMs can accelerate coding and process large datasets; no measured runtime, token use, monetary cost, energy, or human verification burden
Efficiency or cost results.anchor: coding-opportunities section, p. 200, and whole-paper audit

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Substantial conceptual discussion of training-data bias, cultural bias, hallucination, opacity, accountability, data leakage, anonymization, external API disclosure, participant privacy, open-source models, and human control. The article proposes high privacy standards and anonymized access in Social Verbatim, but reports no ethics protocol for an LLM study because none was conducted.
Ethics and privacy treatment.anchor: challenges, recommendations, and Social Verbatim sections, pp. 204-212

Reproducibility resources.value: Official diamond-open-access article and conventional references; no review protocol, search log, included-study dataset, extraction file, code, prompts, model configuration, or implemented LLM extension is released with this article. The current Social Verbatim website is named.

Author-reported limitations.value: No limitations of the article's review method or evidentiary selection are reported. The author does explicitly characterize LLM limitations—lack of genuine understanding, weak context, inconsistency, hallucination, bias, opacity, privacy/security, and replicability—and presents Social Verbatim LLM integration as future development rather than a completed evaluation.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concerns: absent review methods prevent assessment of completeness or selection bias; the literature tables mix classification, coding, software, and methodological papers without a declared appraisal framework; several technical descriptions conflate zero-shot prompting, training, and fine-tuning; broad claims about efficiency and depth are not tested here; and the 15-user formative study concerns the earlier non-LLM tool, so it cannot validate the proposed LLM integration. These are reviewer judgments, not author claims.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: Reviewer assessment of the complete official PDF, especially pp. 199-204 and 210-213

Relationship to prior papers.value: Extends the author's CS-Transcribe/Social Verbatim development line and cites the prior 15-interview tool study; reviews Dai et al., CHALET/QualiGPT, Thematic-LM, MindCoder, Argument2Code and related systems without replicating them.
Relationship to prior papers.anchor: Introduction, Tables 1-2, and Social Verbatim section, pp. 196, 200-204, 210-212

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Adjacent design evidence for VoiceTrace-style requirements—prompt/procedure traceability, open models, privacy, human interpretive authority, feedback, and keeping analysts close to data. It does not close VoiceTrace, WarrantBench, or StopTA because the LLM functionality is prospective and no source coverage, warrant-quality, stability, or stopping outcome is evaluated.
